input.text: If the National Museum tells China's story, the Capital Museum tells Beijing's — and often, more comfortably. Founded in nineteen eighty-one and reborn in a striking new building in two thousand six — a hall of stone and a bronze-walled drum that nods to ancient Chinese forms — it gathers the city's own treasures: Shang and Zhou bronzes, imperial porcelain, folk crafts, and superb galleries walking you through how a little frontier town called Ji became Dadu, then Peking, then Beijing. The galleries are airy, the lighting kind, and the crowds a fraction of the big names — if the National Museum's queue defeated you, this is the dignified alternative. Look for the old Beijing street-life reconstruction downstairs: shopfronts, cricket cages, and courtyard sounds — old Peking rebuilt in a hallway. An hour and a half covers the highlights; the coin and porcelain rooms reward the slow.
